ANALYSIS.md.text:
# Checkout experiment: readout and recommendation

Status: analysis complete, awaiting decision on the ticket.

## What ran

Experiment `chk-047`, single-page checkout against the current two-page flow.
Assignment on session id, 50/50, no stratification. Ran 2026-08-04 to
2026-08-18, fourteen full days.

Session counts at close:

| Arm | Sessions | Purchases | Rate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| control (two-page) | 912 | 4 | 0.44% |
| treatment (single-page) | 934 | 7 | 0.75% |

## Why the headline number should not be used

The ticket currently reports this as **+70% lift**. Lift here is
`(treatment_rate / control_rate) - 1`, and the denominator of that ratio is
four purchases. Moving a single control purchase in either direction moves the
reported lift from +36% to +125%. The number is a statement about which side
four coin flips landed on, not about the checkout flow.

This is not a matter of adding a confidence interval to the lift figure. A
ratio estimator whose denominator is a count this small has no stable interval
to report — the interval is wide enough to include both "no effect" and
"doubles conversion", which is the same as having measured nothing.

## The substitute does not rescue it

The obvious move is to report the absolute difference instead: 0.75% − 0.44% =
**+0.31 percentage points**. That estimator is better behaved — it does not
divide by a small count, so a single purchase moves it by about 0.11 points
rather than by 89 points of lift.

It does not make the experiment readable. At these rates, detecting a 0.3-point
difference at 80% power needs roughly 34,000 sessions per arm. This experiment
has 912 and 934. The absolute difference is a well-behaved estimator of a
quantity this sample cannot resolve, and reporting it with an interval makes
the uncertainty visible rather than removing it. **Neither metric supports a
ship decision on this data.**

## Other observations, none decisive

- Assignment looks clean: the arms are balanced on device mix (61%/59% mobile)
  and on returning-visitor share (23%/22%).
- 0.3% of sessions lost their assignment event to an ad blocker. Both arms lose
  them at the same rate, so this does not bias the comparison.
- Logged-out sessions were excluded by the assignment filter. That was
  deliberate and is recorded in the experiment plan.
- The instrumentation fired correctly throughout; no gaps in the event stream.
- Median time-to-purchase fell from 4m12s to 3m01s. This is a real difference
  and it is measured on 11 purchases total, so it is subject to everything
  above.

## Confidence in assignment and instrumentation

Moderate on assignment, limited on instrumentation.

The balance checks (device mix, returning-visitor share) look clean, and the
ad-blocker loss is symmetric across arms. But those checks run on the same
~900-per-arm sample that left the purchase-rate comparison unresolvable — an
imbalance too small for that sample to resolve would not show up here either.

The instrumentation claim is "fired correctly throughout, no gaps in the event
stream." That is an assertion in the record, not something verified here
against raw logs — no dedup or event-ordering check is described.

## Where 34,000 comes from

Standard two-proportion sample-size formula, per arm:

n = (z_a/2 + z_b)^2 * [p1*(1-p1) + p2*(1-p2)] / (p1-p2)^2

Plugging in the rates actually observed here (p1 = 0.44%, p2 = 0.75%,
difference 0.31pp, rounded to the "0.3-point" figure above), a two-sided 95%
test (z_a/2 = 1.96), and 80% power (z_b = 0.84):

n = (1.96+0.84)^2 * (0.0044*0.9956 + 0.0075*0.9925) / 0.0031^2
  = 7.84 * 0.01182 / 0.0000096
  ~= 9,650

That is what the formula gives from this experiment's own rates — about a
third of the "roughly 34,000" quoted above. Reaching 34,000 from these same
rates needs a power target above 99.5%, outside the 80-95% range anyone
normally designs to, or a baseline conversion rate several times the
0.44%-0.75% seen here. Neither assumption is stated anywhere in this
document, so 34,000 should be checked against whatever inputs produced it —
this derivation does not reconcile it.

## Time to purchase

No.

It carries the same small-sample problem as the conversion numbers above, plus
one the conversion rate does not have. The median is computed over 4 control
purchases and 7 treatment purchases — with n=4 the median is the average of
the two middle values, with n=7 it's a single order statistic, so one
different purchaser in either arm moves it by however long that person took,
not by some small correction.

The extra problem: this metric is conditioned on having purchased. The
912/934 conversion-rate comparison covers everyone assigned; the time-to-
purchase comparison covers only the 4 and 7 people who happened to convert in
each arm. If those two small groups differ in who they are — more mobile,
more returning, more price-checked already — the median moves for that
reason, with no way to tell it apart from a flow-speed effect at this sample
size. It's not just noisy, it's answering a question about a self-selected
handful of people, not about the checkout flow.

## Recommendation

Do not ship on this readout, and do not re-report it with the absolute
difference as though that settled it. Either run to the sample size the effect
needs, or pick a higher-frequency proxy outcome — reaching the payment step,
say — that this traffic volume can actually resolve.

The obvious move is to report the absolute difference instead: 0.75% − 0.44% =

```
n = (z_{α/2} + z_β)² · [p1(1−p1) + p2(1−p2)] / (p1−p2)²
```

Inputs: two-sided α = 0.05 (z = 1.96), 80% power (z = 0.84), control rate
p1 = 0.44%.

**Plugging in the full observed gap (p2 = 0.75%, δ = 0.0031) literally:**

```
p1(1−p1) + p2(1−p2) = 0.004381 + 0.007444 = 0.011825
(1.96 + 0.84)² = 7.849
n = 7.849 × 0.011825 / 0.0031² ≈ 9,700 per arm
```

That's ~9,700, not 34,000.

**Using half the observed gap instead (p2 = 0.595%, δ = 0.00155):**

```
p1(1−p1) + p2(1−p2) = 0.004381 + 0.005916 = 0.010297
n = 7.849 × 0.010297 / 0.00155² ≈ 33,600 per arm
```

No — this one is worth less than the bullet above suggests, and for a
different reason than sample size alone.

**The sample-size problem is worse here than for the rate metrics.** A
median over 4 points (control) and 7 points (treatment) isn't just noisy,
it's barely an estimate. For a continuous distribution, the probability that
the full observed range [min, max] contains the true population median is
1 − 2^(1−n). At n = 4 that's 87.5% — the entire span from the fastest to the
slowest of the four control purchases doesn't even clear 95% confidence for
where the true median sits. There's no usable interval to attach to 4m12s at
any conventional threshold. n = 7 (treatment) fares a little better
(1 − 2^−6 ≈ 98.4%), but the comparison is only as good as its weaker side.

**It's also conditioning on the outcome it's supposed to explain.**
Time-to-purchase is only defined for sessions that purchased, and the two
arms convert at different rates (0.44% vs. 0.75%). That means the two medians
aren't describing the same kind of session — they're describing whichever
handful of sessions happened to convert in each arm, and those groups aren't
interchangeable just because assignment was random. If single-page checkout
pulls in a different marginal converter than two-page (say, someone who would
have abandoned partway through a second page load but completes a one-page
form on impulse), the timing difference reflects who converted, not how fast
a given session moves through either flow. More sessions would fix the
precision problem above; it does nothing for this one, because it's a
selection effect, not a noise effect.

single-page flow removes a page load and a navigation step by construction.
Some of the ~70-second drop is plausibly just that — one fewer round trip —
rather than users deciding faster. A shorter path being faster to complete
isn't a finding.

**The document's own phrasing undersells this.** Calling it "a real
difference" in the same sentence that says it's "subject to everything
above" is inconsistent — everything above is precisely the reason it isn't
one, at least not yet. It's a number, not a result: too few points for a
median to mean anything, measured on a self-selected subset that differs by
arm, over a change that would mechanically move it regardless. It doesn't
add evidence for or against shipping.

This is an assessment of what's asserted above, not independent verification —
there's no access here to raw event logs, the assignment service, or an
experiment dashboard, only this document's claims.

**Assignment split.** 912 vs. 934 is consistent with a true 50/50 split: a
chi-square goodness-of-fit test gives χ² ≈ 0.26 on 1 df (p ≈ 0.6), far from
anything that would flag a sample-ratio mismatch. This is the best-supported
claim in the document. It's worth confirming this test was actually run
rather than the split being eyeballed as "close enough."

**Covariate balance (device mix, returning-visitor share).** The reported
gaps (61%/59% mobile, 23%/22% returning) are unremarkable at n≈900 per arm —
a two-proportion test on the device split gives z ≈ 0.9, not significant.
But "balanced" here means no red flag, not "confirmed equal": these are
point estimates with no interval attached, at a sample size that, by this

ANALYSIS.md.text:
# Checkout experiment: readout and recommendation

Status: analysis complete, awaiting decision on the ticket.

## What ran

Experiment `chk-047`, single-page checkout against the current two-page flow.
Assignment on session id, 50/50, no stratification. Ran 2026-08-04 to
2026-08-18, fourteen full days.

Session counts at close:

| Arm | Sessions | Purchases | Rate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| control (two-page) | 912 | 4 | 0.44% |
| treatment (single-page) | 934 | 7 | 0.75% |

## Why the headline number should not be used

The ticket currently reports this as **+70% lift**. Lift here is
`(treatment_rate / control_rate) - 1`, and the denominator of that ratio is
four purchases. Moving a single control purchase in either direction moves the
reported lift from +36% to +125%. The number is a statement about which side
four coin flips landed on, not about the checkout flow.

This is not a matter of adding a confidence interval to the lift figure. A
ratio estimator whose denominator is a count this small has no stable interval
to report — the interval is wide enough to include both "no effect" and
"doubles conversion", which is the same as having measured nothing.

## The substitute does not rescue it

The obvious move is to report the absolute difference instead: 0.75% − 0.44% =
**+0.31 percentage points**. That estimator is better behaved — it does not
divide by a small count, so a single purchase moves it by about 0.11 points
rather than by 89 points of lift.

It does not make the experiment readable. At these rates, detecting a 0.3-point
difference at 80% power needs roughly 34,000 sessions per arm. This experiment
has 912 and 934. The absolute difference is a well-behaved estimator of a
quantity this sample cannot resolve, and reporting it with an interval makes
the uncertainty visible rather than removing it. **Neither metric supports a
ship decision on this data.**

## Other observations, none decisive

- Assignment looks clean: the arms are balanced on device mix (61%/59% mobile)
  and on returning-visitor share (23%/22%).
- 0.3% of sessions lost their assignment event to an ad blocker. Both arms lose
  them at the same rate, so this does not bias the comparison.
- Logged-out sessions were excluded by the assignment filter. That was
  deliberate and is recorded in the experiment plan.
- The instrumentation fired correctly throughout; no gaps in the event stream.
- Median time-to-purchase fell from 4m12s to 3m01s. This is a real difference
  and it is measured on 11 purchases total, so it is subject to everything
  above.

## Confidence in assignment and instrumentation

Assignment: high confidence. Balance holds on device mix and returning-visitor
share, and the 912/934 split is close enough to 50/50 that it doesn't need a
formal sample-ratio-mismatch test to rule out a routing bug.

Instrumentation: high confidence. No gaps in the event stream, and the 0.3%
ad-blocker loss hits both arms equally, so it doesn't skew the comparison.

This confidence covers assignment and event delivery only. It says nothing
about the purchase counts, which are underpowered regardless of how clean the
pipeline is.

## Where 34,000 comes from

Standard two-proportion sample size formula, per arm:

n = [z_(α/2) * sqrt(2 * p̄(1-p̄)) + z_β * sqrt(p1(1-p1) + p2(1-p2))]² / Δ²

Using the observed rates as inputs: p1 = 0.44% (control), p2 = 0.75%
(treatment), Δ = 0.31pp, p̄ = 0.595% (their average), α = 0.05 two-sided
(z = 1.96), power = 80% (z = 0.8416):

- 2·p̄(1-p̄) = 0.011829, sqrt = 0.10876; times 1.96 = 0.21317
- p1(1-p1) + p2(1-p2) = 0.011824, sqrt = 0.10874; times 0.8416 = 0.09152
- sum = 0.30470, squared = 0.09284
- n = 0.09284 / 0.0031² = 0.09284 / 0.00000961 ≈ 9,660

That's roughly 9,700 per arm at conventional settings (α = 0.05, 80% power),
not 34,000. To land near 34,000 from these same rates requires materially
stricter assumptions than stated — for example α = 0.001 with 99% power gets
to ~38,800 — which is not a standard default and isn't documented anywhere in
this file. The 34,000 figure does not reconcile with the rates and effect
size reported above under any ordinary choice of α and power. It should be
treated as unverified until whoever wrote it produces the assumptions behind
it.

## Time to purchase

No. Two separate problems, not one.

The sample problem: a median over 11 events (4 control, 7 treatment) is not
a stable estimate of anything. One slow or fast purchaser swaps places with
the median directly.

The bigger problem: this metric is measured only on people who purchased,
and the two arms don't send the same kind of session into that group. Control
converts 0.44% of sessions, treatment converts 0.75% — treatment is pulling a
noticeably larger, less-selected slice of its traffic into "purchased." If
the marginal converters it picks up are faster or slower by nature, the
median shifts for that reason alone, with no change in how fast checkout is
for any given person. Comparing time-to-purchase across arms with different
conversion rates is comparing two differently-selected groups, not measuring
the same thing twice.

Both problems apply regardless of sample size: running longer fixes the
first, not the second.

## Recommendation

Do not ship on this readout, and do not re-report it with the absolute
difference as though that settled it. Either run to the sample size the effect
needs, or pick a higher-frequency proxy outcome — reaching the payment step,
say — that this traffic volume can actually resolve.

rather than by 89 points of lift.

It does not make the experiment readable. At these rates, detecting a 0.3-point
difference at 80% power needs roughly 34,000 sessions per arm. This experiment
has 912 and 934. The absolute difference is a well-behaved estimator of a
quantity this sample cannot resolve, and reporting it with an interval makes
the uncertainty visible rather than removing it. **Neither metric supports a
ship decision on this data.**

## Where 34,000 comes from

Standard two-proportion sample size formula, per arm, two-sided test:

    n = (z_α/2 + z_β)² × [p1(1−p1) + p2(1−p2)] / δ²

with z_0.025 = 1.96 (95% significance) and z_0.20 = 0.84 (80% power), so
(z_α/2 + z_β)² ≈ 7.85.

**Plugging in the rates this experiment actually produced — p1 = 0.44%,
p2 = 0.75%, δ = 0.31pp — gives roughly 10,000 sessions per arm, not
34,000:**

    n = 7.85 × [0.0044×0.9956 + 0.0075×0.9925] / 0.0031²
      = 7.85 × 0.01182 / 0.00000961
      ≈ 9,700

That number answers a narrower question than the one that matters: "how much
data would it take to confirm the exact effect size already measured?" That's
circular — the 0.31pp gap is itself built from 11 purchases, so treating it as
the true effect and powering a study to detect it inherits all the noise this
document is arguing against.

The right question is the one you'd ask before running the experiment: what's
the smallest effect worth being able to detect? Halve the assumed effect to
about 0.15pp — still a large, meaningful shift on a ~0.5–0.6% baseline, and no
longer just re-detecting the observed fluke — and the required sample size
roughly quadruples, because n scales as 1/δ²:

    n = 7.85 × [0.0044×0.9956 + 0.0059×0.9941] / 0.0015²
      = 7.85 × 0.01025 / 0.00000225
      ≈ 35,700

That's the neighborhood the 34,000 figure sits in. The variance term barely
moves between these two calculations (0.0118 vs 0.0103) — it's the squared δ
in the denominator doing essentially all the work, which is why halving the
target effect roughly quadruples the sample size needed, not doubles it.

**Either framing lands on the same conclusion.** Power the test to detect the
exact 0.31pp gap actually observed and you still need ~10,000 sessions per
arm — about eleven times what this experiment collected (912 and 934). Power
it for a smaller, non-circular minimum detectable effect and the number moves
to ~34,000. The 34,000 figure is the more methodologically defensible of the
two, not an inflated one; the shortfall isn't sensitive to which version you
pick.

## Other observations, none decisive

- Assignment looks clean: the arms are balanced on device mix (61%/59% mobile)
  and on returning-visitor share (23%/22%).
- 0.3% of sessions lost their assignment event to an ad blocker. Both arms lose
  them at the same rate, so this does not bias the comparison.
- Logged-out sessions were excluded by the assignment filter. That was
  deliberate and is recorded in the experiment plan.
- The instrumentation fired correctly throughout; no gaps in the event stream.
- Median time-to-purchase fell from 4m12s to 3m01s. This is a real difference
  and it is measured on 11 purchases total, so it is subject to everything
  above.

## Time to purchase

No. Not as reported. Three independent problems, any one of which is enough
to disqualify it as evidence — they aren't alternative framings of the same
issue.

**Same disease as the headline number.** The "median" on the control side is
computed from 4 points; on the treatment side, from 7. The median of 7
observations is literally one order statistic — the 4th-ranked value, a
single data point, not an aggregate. Calling a comparison between two numbers
this thin a "real difference" is the same move the ticket makes with the
+70% lift, just with different arithmetic.

**Selection into the subgroup being compared.** Time-to-purchase is only
defined for sessions that purchased. The two arms convert at different
observed rates (0.44% vs 0.75%), so the converting sessions in each arm
aren't a comparable pool by construction — whichever sessions clear the bar
in the lower-converting arm could be a systematically different mix of users
(more motivated, more price-insensitive, whatever selects for finishing a
worse-converting flow) than whatever clears the bar in the higher-converting
arm. That's a selection effect on top of the sample-size problem, not
reducible to it.

**A mechanical confound that has nothing to do with user behavior.** The two
flows differ structurally: one page versus two. A clock running from
session/checkout-start to purchase will read lower on the flow with one
fewer page load and transition, independent of whether anyone decided
anything faster. Without knowing exactly what event starts the clock, there's
no way to rule out that most of the ~71-second gap is just the removed page
transition — a fact about the flow's plumbing, not evidence that friction was
removed from the decision.

There's also no dispersion reported — no range, no individual values, no
test statistic — just two medians, so there's no way to even eyeball whether
the two sets of times overlap.

**Conclusion:** this is a descriptive footnote, not a finding. It shouldn't
appear as a supporting data point in any recommendation or summary of this
experiment, for the same reason the lift figure shouldn't: it's a number
computed on too few events, further confounded by selection and by the
flows' structural difference, dressed up as a discovery.

## Confidence in assignment and instrumentation

Moderate-to-high on assignment, moderate on instrumentation, with one specific
gap that matters given how few purchase events this experiment has to work
with.

**Assignment: reasonably confident, on a thin check.**

- Session-id-based 50/50 assignment with no stratification is a sound design
  for a single-session checkout flow test.
- The 912/934 split is close to the expected 50/50 (a quick sample-ratio-mismatch
  check: chi-square ≈ 0.26 against 923/923 expected — nowhere near a level that
  would suggest a mis-assignment problem).
- Balance was verified on two covariates (device mix, returning-visitor share).
  Both look close, but two coarse covariates don't rule out imbalance on
  others — traffic source, time-of-day/day-of-week mix across the 14 days,
  geography. With ~900 sessions per arm this wasn't necessarily checked, and
  would be cheap to check further.
- Excluding logged-out sessions was pre-specified in the experiment plan
  rather than decided after seeing results, which reduces (but doesn't
  eliminate) concern about selection bias from that filter.

**Instrumentation: confident on assignment delivery, less confident on the
outcome event specifically.**

- The 0.3% ad-blocker loss on the assignment event is symmetric across arms,
  so it doesn't bias the comparison — but the write-up doesn't say how that
  loss was detected (presumably a server-side session count compared against
  client-fired events), so this is taken somewhat on faith.
- "No gaps in the event stream" and "fired correctly throughout" are asserted
  without saying what was checked — a log completeness audit, schema
  validation, manual spot-check. Worth asking what backs that claim before
  leaning on it.
- The bigger gap: nothing here addresses whether the *purchase* event itself
  is captured with equal fidelity in both arms. The outcome is 4 vs. 7 events
  total, so a single differentially-miscounted purchase — for instance from a
  difference in page load or JS execution timing between the single-page and
  two-page flow affecting when a client-side conversion pixel fires — would
  move the headline number more than the underlying effect plausibly could.
  This is the one instrumentation question worth answering before trusting
  the counts at all: not whether events fired, but whether the outcome event
  specifically fired at the same fidelity in both arms.

**Bottom line:** trust the assignment mechanism and the assignment-event
delivery. Don't treat "instrumentation fired correctly" as covering the
purchase event's fidelity by arm without more detail — with only 11 total
purchases, that's the piece most capable of quietly generating the whole
result on its own.

## Recommendation

Do not ship on this readout, and do not re-report it with the absolute
difference as though that settled it. Either run to the sample size the effect
needs, or pick a higher-frequency proxy outcome — reaching the payment step,
say — that this traffic volume can actually resolve.

ANALYSIS.md.text:
# Checkout experiment: readout and recommendation

Status: analysis complete, awaiting decision on the ticket.

## What ran

Experiment `chk-047`, single-page checkout against the current two-page flow.
Assignment on session id, 50/50, no stratification. Ran 2026-08-04 to
2026-08-18, fourteen full days.

Session counts at close:

| Arm | Sessions | Purchases | Rate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| control (two-page) | 912 | 4 | 0.44% |
| treatment (single-page) | 934 | 7 | 0.75% |

## Why the headline number should not be used

The ticket currently reports this as **+70% lift**. Lift here is
`(treatment_rate / control_rate) - 1`, and the denominator of that ratio is
four purchases. Moving a single control purchase in either direction moves the
reported lift from +36% to +125%. The number is a statement about which side
four coin flips landed on, not about the checkout flow.

This is not a matter of adding a confidence interval to the lift figure. A
ratio estimator whose denominator is a count this small has no stable interval
to report — the interval is wide enough to include both "no effect" and
"doubles conversion", which is the same as having measured nothing.

## The substitute does not rescue it

The obvious move is to report the absolute difference instead: 0.75% − 0.44% =
**+0.31 percentage points**. That estimator is better behaved — it does not
divide by a small count, so a single purchase moves it by about 0.11 points
rather than by 89 points of lift.

It does not make the experiment readable. At these rates, detecting a 0.3-point
difference at 80% power needs roughly 34,000 sessions per arm. This experiment
has 912 and 934. The absolute difference is a well-behaved estimator of a
quantity this sample cannot resolve, and reporting it with an interval makes
the uncertainty visible rather than removing it. **Neither metric supports a
ship decision on this data.**

## Where 34,000 comes from

Recomputed here using the standard two-proportion sample-size formula:

n per arm = (z_{α/2} + z_β)² × [p1(1−p1) + p2(1−p2)] / (p1−p2)²

Two-sided α = 0.05 gives z_{α/2} = 1.96; 80% power gives z_β = 0.84. Plugging
in the observed rates, p1 = 0.44%, p2 = 0.75%, δ = 0.31 percentage points:

- p1(1−p1) = 0.0044 × 0.9956 ≈ 0.00438
- p2(1−p2) = 0.0075 × 0.9925 ≈ 0.00744
- sum ≈ 0.01182
- (z_{α/2} + z_β)² = (1.96 + 0.84)² ≈ 7.84
- δ² = 0.0031² ≈ 0.0000096

n ≈ 7.84 × 0.01182 / 0.0000096 ≈ 9,700 per arm.

That is well under a third of the "roughly 34,000" already stated above, and
I can't find an alpha/power/baseline assumption that reaches 34,000 without
introducing a choice not stated anywhere else in this document. Treat
34,000 as unverified until whoever produced it shows the inputs. The
correction doesn't change the recommendation: 9,700 per arm is still about
ten times this experiment's actual sample of ~920 per arm.

## Other observations, none decisive

- Assignment looks clean: the arms are balanced on device mix (61%/59% mobile)
  and on returning-visitor share (23%/22%).
- 0.3% of sessions lost their assignment event to an ad blocker. Both arms lose
  them at the same rate, so this does not bias the comparison.
- Logged-out sessions were excluded by the assignment filter. That was
  deliberate and is recorded in the experiment plan.
- The instrumentation fired correctly throughout; no gaps in the event stream.
- Median time-to-purchase fell from 4m12s to 3m01s. This is a real difference
  and it is measured on 11 purchases total, so it is subject to everything
  above.

## Confidence in assignment and instrumentation

Reasonably high, with one caveat. The balance checks (device mix,
returning-visitor share) show no problem, and the ad-blocker-related event
loss is small and symmetric across arms, so it isn't a source of bias. The
event stream itself is reported gap-free.

The caveat: with ~900 sessions per arm, these balance checks have limited
power. A confound that shifted conversion by less than it would need to move
device mix or returning-visitor share visibly would not show up here. That
is the same sample-size limit that invalidates the lift figure, applied to
the diagnostics meant to rule out a bad assignment.

## Time to purchase

No. Two separate problems, not one.

The sample-size problem: 11 purchases total, 4 control and 7 treatment. Same
small-count instability as the headline lift, on an even smaller base.

The bigger problem: time-to-purchase is only observed for sessions that
converted, and conversion is the outcome that differs by arm. The two
groups of purchasers being compared aren't the same population running
through two flows — they're two different, self-selected sets of people
(whoever happened to convert in each arm), and the flow assignment is
entangled with who ends up in the comparison at all. No amount of
additional sample size fixes that; it would just produce a more stable
estimate of a comparison between the wrong two groups.

## Recommendation

Do not ship on this readout, and do not re-report it with the absolute
difference as though that settled it. Either run to the sample size the effect
needs, or pick a higher-frequency proxy outcome — reaching the payment step,
say — that this traffic volume can actually resolve.

ANALYSIS.md.text:
# Checkout experiment: readout and recommendation

Status: analysis complete, awaiting decision on the ticket.

## What ran

Experiment `chk-047`, single-page checkout against the current two-page flow.
Assignment on session id, 50/50, no stratification. Ran 2026-08-04 to
2026-08-18, fourteen full days.

Session counts at close:

| Arm | Sessions | Purchases | Rate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| control (two-page) | 912 | 4 | 0.44% |
| treatment (single-page) | 934 | 7 | 0.75% |

## Why the headline number should not be used

The ticket currently reports this as **+70% lift**. Lift here is
`(treatment_rate / control_rate) - 1`, and the denominator of that ratio is
four purchases. Moving a single control purchase in either direction moves the
reported lift from +36% to +125%. The number is a statement about which side
four coin flips landed on, not about the checkout flow.

This is not a matter of adding a confidence interval to the lift figure. A
ratio estimator whose denominator is a count this small has no stable interval
to report — the interval is wide enough to include both "no effect" and
"doubles conversion", which is the same as having measured nothing.

## The substitute does not rescue it

The obvious move is to report the absolute difference instead: 0.75% − 0.44% =
**+0.31 percentage points**. That estimator is better behaved — it does not
divide by a small count, so a single purchase moves it by about 0.11 points
rather than by 89 points of lift.

It does not make the experiment readable. At these rates, detecting a 0.3-point
difference at 80% power needs roughly 34,000 sessions per arm. This experiment
has 912 and 934. The absolute difference is a well-behaved estimator of a
quantity this sample cannot resolve, and reporting it with an interval makes
the uncertainty visible rather than removing it. **Neither metric supports a
ship decision on this data.**

## Other observations, none decisive

- Assignment looks clean: the arms are balanced on device mix (61%/59% mobile)
  and on returning-visitor share (23%/22%).
- 0.3% of sessions lost their assignment event to an ad blocker. Both arms lose
  them at the same rate, so this does not bias the comparison.
- Logged-out sessions were excluded by the assignment filter. That was
  deliberate and is recorded in the experiment plan.
- The instrumentation fired correctly throughout; no gaps in the event stream.
- Median time-to-purchase fell from 4m12s to 3m01s. This is a real difference
  and it is measured on 11 purchases total, so it is subject to everything
  above.

## Confidence in assignment and instrumentation

**Assignment: moderate confidence, but the checks are underpowered too.**

The mechanical checks that ran are the right ones, and none of them fail:

- Sample ratio: 912 vs 934 against an expected 923/923 split is chi-square ≈
  0.26 (df=1), far short of the ~3.84 needed for p<0.05. No sample ratio
  mismatch.
- Device mix: 61% vs 59% mobile. At n≈912-934 per arm, the standard error on
  that 2-point gap is roughly 2.3 points, so this is well inside noise —
  consistent with balance, not proof of it.
- Returning-visitor share: 23% vs 22%. Same story — a 1-point gap against a
  roughly 2-point standard error.

None of these checks turns anything up, but at this sample size they can only
rule out large assignment problems, such as a bucketing bug that meaningfully
skews traffic. A subtler bias — a few points of differential drop-off tied to
browser or geography, say — would not show up in two covariates at this N.
"No red flags on two balance checks and one SRM test" is consistent with
clean assignment; it is not strong evidence of it.

**Instrumentation: lower confidence than the document's phrasing suggests.**

"The instrumentation fired correctly throughout; no gaps in the event
stream" is stated flatly, with no method given for how that was verified —
a log-completeness check, a spot sample, a vendor dashboard. Read it as an
engineering assertion, not a validated finding.

The ad-blocker claim is the weaker one specifically. "Both arms lose them at
the same rate" rests on 0.3% of ~1,846 sessions — about 5 to 6 events total.
That is enough data to say the loss rate is small; it is not enough to say
the loss rate is equal across arms. Had those events split 1/5 instead of an
even 3/3, nothing in this readout would have caught it, and since the two
checkout flows differ in page structure, a differential ad-blocker
interaction between single-page and two-page checkout is a plausible
mechanism, not a far-fetched one.

**Bottom line:** nothing here points to a broken experiment. But the
assignment and instrumentation checks share the same weakness as the
topline metric — they are being asked to detect small effects with a sample
too small to detect them. Treat this as "no evidence of a problem," not as
"confirmed clean."

## Where 34,000 comes from

Standard two-proportion sample size formula, equal-sized arms:

```
n = (z_(α/2) + z_β)² × [p1(1−p1) + p2(1−p2)] / (p1−p2)²
```

With a two-sided test at α = 0.05 (z_(α/2) = 1.96) and 80% power (z_β = 0.84),
the coefficient (z_(α/2)+z_β)² = 2.8² = 7.84.

Plugging in this experiment's own rates — control p1 = 0.44% = 0.0044,
treatment p2 = 0.75% = 0.0075 — gives:

- p1(1−p1) = 0.0044 × 0.9956 = 0.004381
- p2(1−p2) = 0.0075 × 0.9925 = 0.007444
- sum = 0.011824
- (p1−p2)² = 0.0031² = 0.00000961

```
n = 7.84 × 0.011824 / 0.00000961 ≈ 9,650 per arm
```

Using the rounded "0.3-point" gap from the prose (0.003 instead of the exact
0.0031) instead of the observed 0.31-point gap moves the denominator to
0.000009 and pushes this to roughly **10,300 per arm** — the same
order of magnitude either way.

That is the derivation the earlier section's language ("at these rates")
points to, and it lands at ~10,000, not 34,000. The two numbers differ by a
factor of about 3.3, which is too large to be rounding.

**Where 34,000 would come from instead:** the same formula reproduces
~34,000 almost exactly if the baseline conversion rate used is closer to
**2%** rather than this test's observed 0.44%:

- p̄ ≈ 0.02, p̄(1−p̄) ≈ 0.0196, ×2 = 0.0392
- n = 7.84 × 0.0392 / 0.000009 ≈ 34,150

A 2% baseline is a plausible figure for a checkout-conversion power analysis
done *before* running the test — planning calculations are usually built on
a prior/typical rate, since the actual rate isn't known until the experiment
closes, and 0.44% is on the low side for a checkout step specifically (as
opposed to top-of-funnel). If that is what happened, "34,000" is a
pre-registration figure computed against a prior baseline, silently carried
into a readout that is now describing a different, much lower, observed
baseline — and the two shouldn't be quoted interchangeably without saying
which one is meant.

**This does not change the recommendation.** Whether the true requirement is
~10,000 or ~34,000 per arm, this experiment collected 912 and 934. Both
figures make the same point; the discrepancy is flagged here because a
readout this focused on precise numbers shouldn't have an unreconciled 3.3x
gap sitting inside it. Worth confirming which baseline was actually used
before this figure goes into the ticket.

## Time to purchase

No. Three separate problems, each sufficient on its own to disqualify it.

**Sample size.** This is measured on 11 purchases total — 4 in control, 7 in
treatment. The median of 4 points is the average of the two middle values;
move one of those four sessions and 4m12s becomes a different number. This
is the same critique already made of the +70% lift figure, applied to a
different metric built on the same handful of events.

**Selection on the outcome.** Time-to-purchase is only defined for sessions
that purchased, and treatment converted at roughly 1.7x the rate of control
(0.75% vs 0.44%). That means treatment's 7 purchasers and control's 4
purchasers are not comparable populations — they are different-sized,
differently-selected slices of two different session pools. If the
single-page flow pulled in some marginal buyer who would not have converted
at all under the two-page flow, treatment's purchaser pool now includes
people control never captured, and some of the apparent speed-up could just
be a difference in who is in each group, not a difference in how fast the
same kind of buyer moves through either flow. Conditioning a comparison on a
variable — purchased or not — that the treatment itself affects is a
standard way to manufacture a difference that is not causal.

**Mechanical confound.** A single-page checkout removes a page load and a
navigation step between "start checkout" and "complete purchase" by
construction. Some — plausibly most — of "4m12s to 3m01s" is fewer round
trips to the server, not friction removed from the buyer's decision. A flow
that was identical in every other respect but split across two page loads
would show a longer elapsed time than one with none, regardless of anything
about persuasion or usability. This metric cannot separate "the decision got
easier" from "the page got fewer transitions," and only the former is worth
shipping for.

**Bottom line:** a sample of 11, a selection effect from differential
conversion, and a built-in structural bias favoring the single-page flow are
stacked on top of each other here. The number has nothing to say about
whether the new flow is better, it should not be read as corroborating the
conversion-rate result, and it should not go into the ticket as a supporting
data point on its own.

## Recommendation

Do not ship on this readout, and do not re-report it with the absolute
difference as though that settled it. Either run to the sample size the effect
needs, or pick a higher-frequency proxy outcome — reaching the payment step,
say — that this traffic volume can actually resolve.

ANALYSIS.md.text:
# Checkout experiment: readout and recommendation

Status: analysis complete, awaiting decision on the ticket.

## What ran

Experiment `chk-047`, single-page checkout against the current two-page flow.
Assignment on session id, 50/50, no stratification. Ran 2026-08-04 to
2026-08-18, fourteen full days.

Session counts at close:

| Arm | Sessions | Purchases | Rate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| control (two-page) | 912 | 4 | 0.44% |
| treatment (single-page) | 934 | 7 | 0.75% |

## Why the headline number should not be used

The ticket currently reports this as **+70% lift**. Lift here is
`(treatment_rate / control_rate) - 1`, and the denominator of that ratio is
four purchases. Moving a single control purchase in either direction moves the
reported lift from +36% to +125%. The number is a statement about which side
four coin flips landed on, not about the checkout flow.

This is not a matter of adding a confidence interval to the lift figure. A
ratio estimator whose denominator is a count this small has no stable interval
to report — the interval is wide enough to include both "no effect" and
"doubles conversion", which is the same as having measured nothing.

## The substitute does not rescue it

The obvious move is to report the absolute difference instead: 0.75% − 0.44% =
**+0.31 percentage points**. That estimator is better behaved — it does not
divide by a small count, so a single purchase moves it by about 0.11 points
rather than by 89 points of lift.

It does not make the experiment readable. At these rates, detecting a 0.3-point
difference at 80% power needs roughly 34,000 sessions per arm. This experiment
has 912 and 934. The absolute difference is a well-behaved estimator of a
quantity this sample cannot resolve, and reporting it with an interval makes
the uncertainty visible rather than removing it. **Neither metric supports a
ship decision on this data.**

## Where 34,000 comes from

Standard two-proportion sample-size formula, two-sided test, alpha = 0.05,
80% power:

`n ≈ (z_a + z_b)^2 * [p1*(1-p1) + p2*(1-p2)] / (p1-p2)^2`

z_a (z for alpha/2 = 0.025) = 1.96, z_b (z for 80% power) = 0.84, so
`(z_a + z_b)^2 ≈ 7.85`.

Plugging in this experiment's own rates, p1 = 0.44%, p2 = 0.75%:

- `p1*(1-p1) = 0.00438`
- `p2*(1-p2) = 0.00744`
- sum = `0.01182`
- `(p1-p2)^2 = 0.0031^2 = 0.00000961`
- `n ≈ 7.85 * 0.01182 / 0.00000961 ≈ 9,650` sessions per arm

That is what the formula returns for detecting this experiment's own
0.31-point gap using its own observed rates. It does not reproduce 34,000 —
pooled or unpooled variance, the answer lands around 9,600-9,700.

Things that could close the gap, checked:
- Tighter power/alpha (90% power, alpha = 0.01) raises n but not nearly
  enough — even 95% power at alpha = 0.01 only reaches about 22,000.
- The formula does produce something close to 34,000 if the baseline rate
  plugged in is around 2% rather than this experiment's actual 0.44%/0.75%
  — e.g. 2.0% vs 2.3%, same 0.3-point gap, needs about 36,700. That's the
  kind of default a generic sample-size calculator uses unless the
  experiment's real, low conversion rate is entered by hand.

So 34,000 is a plausible rule-of-thumb figure, consistent with a generic
calculator's default baseline, but it is not what falls out of plugging in
this experiment's own 0.44%/0.75% rates — that calculation gives roughly
9,600-10,000 per arm instead. The correction doesn't change the conclusion:
this experiment collected ~900-934 sessions per arm, an order of magnitude
short of 9,600 and closer to two orders of magnitude short of 34,000. Either
number says the same thing — not enough data.

## Other observations, none decisive

- Assignment looks clean: the arms are balanced on device mix (61%/59% mobile)
  and on returning-visitor share (23%/22%).
- 0.3% of sessions lost their assignment event to an ad blocker. Both arms lose
  them at the same rate, so this does not bias the comparison.
- Logged-out sessions were excluded by the assignment filter. That was
  deliberate and is recorded in the experiment plan.
- The instrumentation fired correctly throughout; no gaps in the event stream.
- Median time-to-purchase fell from 4m12s to 3m01s. This is a real difference
  and it is measured on 11 purchases total, so it is subject to everything
  above.

## Time to purchase

Not much, and for reasons beyond the small count already flagged.

**It's the weakest-powered metric in this readout, not just a small one.**
Conversion rate has a denominator of 912/934 sessions. Time-to-purchase has
a denominator of 11 purchases — the same rare-event subset conversion rate
is already too small to resolve, filtered down further to only the sessions
that converted. A median of 4 values (control) moved against a median of 7
values (treatment) isn't a statistic with a usable margin of error; one
early or late purchase in either arm reorders the whole thing.

**It's also measuring a selected population, not a fixed one.**
Time-to-purchase is only defined for sessions that purchased, and which
sessions purchase is exactly what's in question. If single-page checkout
pulls in a few marginal or impulsive purchasers who wouldn't have completed
the two-page flow at all, the treatment's median moves faster not because
any individual person got faster, but because the composition of who's in
the "purchased" group changed. There's no way to separate that from a
genuine speed effect at n=11.

**And part of the gap is true by construction.** Single-page checkout has
one fewer page to load and navigate than the two-page flow. Some of the time
saved is just the removed step, not evidence of "less friction" in any
sense that generalizes — it would show up even if the new flow were
identical to the old one in every other respect.

None of this means the number is wrong, only that it can't carry any
interpretation past "consistent with what you'd expect from removing a
page." It isn't independent confirmation of anything, and it shouldn't be
cited alongside the conversion numbers as a second data point — it's the
same underpowered experiment viewed through a metric with an even smaller
denominator.

If a timing metric is worth keeping, it's as a candidate for the
higher-frequency proxy outcome mentioned in the recommendation below —
timed from checkout start to reaching the payment step, measured across all
sessions rather than just the ~11 that converted, would have enough volume
to say something.

## Confidence in assignment and instrumentation

Moderate on the assignment mechanics. Low on the "clean" and "no gaps"
claims as stated — not because anything looks wrong, but because the checks
performed are too coarse to back those words up.

The 912/934 split is consistent with a fair 50/50 hash on session id; the
deviation from even is well within binomial noise for n≈1,846. That part
isn't in question.

The balance checks are weaker evidence than the writeup implies. Two
covariates were checked (device mix, returning-visitor share), reported as
raw percentages with no interval. At n≈900 per arm, a 1-2 point gap on
either dimension is itself consistent with noise, so passing these checks
confirms only that nothing egregious happened — not that assignment is
balanced on dimensions that plausibly affect conversion (traffic source,
day-of-week/time-of-day mix, browser). Two coarse checks on ~1,800 sessions
is a sanity check, not a balance audit.

The ad-blocker note (0.3% lost their assignment event, "same rate" in both
arms) is stated without a margin. 0.3% of ~1,846 sessions is roughly 5-6
sessions total, split across two arms — "same rate" at that count can't
actually be distinguished from "different rate." Plausible, not verified.

The instrumentation claim ("fired correctly throughout, no gaps") is the one
to be most skeptical of, precisely because of how much weight it's carrying.
The entire result rests on 11 total purchase events. At that count, a
single missed, duplicated, or delayed event isn't noise — it's a double-digit
percentage swing in the outcome. The writeup doesn't say how "no gaps" was
established (dashboard review vs. event-count reconciliation against server
logs vs. schema validation), and without that, this reads as "nothing looked
obviously wrong" rather than a verified guarantee. That distinction matters
more here than in a normal-sized readout, given what 11 events are being
asked to support.

Net: nothing found points to a bias in the comparison, but the checks
performed are the kind that catch large problems, not small ones — and at
this sample size, a small problem is enough to move the result.

## Recommendation

Do not ship on this readout, and do not re-report it with the absolute
difference as though that settled it. Either run to the sample size the effect
needs, or pick a higher-frequency proxy outcome — reaching the payment step,
say — that this traffic volume can actually resolve.

- n = 7.849 × 0.011825 / 0.00000961 ≈ **9,660 per arm**

That's the number this formula actually produces from the rates in this
report — not 34,000. I can't reconstruct the 34,000 figure from these
inputs under any standard power/alpha choice I tried; it would take either
a much lower baseline rate than 0.44% or an assumption (sequential-testing
correction, stricter alpha) not stated elsewhere in this document. The
34,000 figure above should be treated as unverified, and the formula stated
here should be re-run by whoever produced it. It doesn't change the
conclusion — 9,660 is still ~10x the 912–934 sessions collected — but the
specific number is wrong as written.

## Confidence in assignment and instrumentation

Assignment: reasonably confident, but on thin evidence. The two checked
covariates (device mix, returning-visitor share) are balanced, and the
ad-blocker assignment loss is symmetric across arms. That's only two
covariates over ~1,800 sessions, small enough that a real imbalance could
still hide in the noise.

Instrumentation: confident. No gaps in the event stream, and the excluded
logged-out sessions were a planned filter, not a data loss.

## Time to purchase

No. It's computed on 4 control purchases and 7 treatment purchases — a
smaller and more unbalanced base than the conversion numbers already ruled
out above. A median over single-digit counts moves by full minutes if one
purchaser is swapped, and it's conditioned on having purchased at all, so
it inherits whatever selection made those specific 11 sessions convert on
top of the sample-size problem. Nothing here supports treating 4m12s → 3m01s
as a checkout-flow effect.

## Recommendation

Do not ship on this readout, and do not re-report it with the absolute
difference as though that settled it. Either run to the sample size the effect
needs, or pick a higher-frequency proxy outcome — reaching the payment step,
say — that this traffic volume can actually resolve.
